entries.definition: The classic Somali popular song style of the 1940s–1970s: a sung melody over the kaban (oud), pentatonic and lyrical, built on balwo and heello love poetry. In present-day usage "qaraami" names both the repertoire of that era and the intimate oud-and-voice manner of performing it.
entries.definitionSo: Heesaha caanka ah ee Soomaalida ee 1940-aadkii ilaa 1970-aadkii: cod iyo kaban, laxan shan-dhawaaqle, oo ku dhisan gabayada balwada iyo heellada.
entries.etymology: From Arabic gharām (passionate love) according to the descriptions of Jama Musse Jama's book Qaraami; not yet checked against a dictionary here. Giannattasio's catalogue also records "qaraami" as a love-themed poetic type (a kind of gabay, 1985). Period: the music is dated mainly to the 1940s–mid-1960s (Jama Musse Jama); "qaraami" is now used for almost any 1950s–70s song (Geeska).
sources: Johnson, John William (1996), Heelloy: Modern Poetry and Songs of the Somali, Haan
African Books Collective, Jama Musse Jama, Qaraami (book description) — https://www.africanbookscollective.com/books/qaraami

Giannattasio, Francesco (1982–1998), Catalogo dei documenti sonori sulla musica somala, Centro Studi Somali — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/bitstream/2307/798/1/Catalogo%20dei%20documenti%20sonori%20sulla%20musica%20somala.pdf
Geeska, The making of Hudeidi — https://www.geeska.com/en/making-hudeidi
Wikipedia, Music of Somalia

entries.definition: The modern Somali song form that grew out of the balwo in the late 1940s and 1950s: longer, more elaborate texts set to new melodies, performed with instruments and broadcast by radio. Giannattasio traces the chain: the kaban, introduced in 1948, gave the short genres (hirwo, dhaanto, wiglo, balwo) a new musical structure, from which the heello emerged; Qarshe's "Lay lay" is said to mark the passage from balwo to heello, and the first political heello dates from 1949. Its rhythm family lives on in the studio's heello groove.
entries.definitionSo: Qaab heeseed casri ah oo ka soo baxay balwada dabayaaqadii 1940-aadkii; magaceedu ka yimid "heelloy heellelloy".
entries.etymology: Usually derived from the vocable refrain "heelloy heellelloy" that opened early performances (Johnson 1996); plausible, but not confirmed in the sources fetched for this review.
sources: Johnson, John William (1996), Heelloy: Modern Poetry and Songs of the Somali, Haan
Giannattasio, Francesco (1988), The study of Somali music: present state — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/handle/2307/984

Giannattasio, Francesco (1982–1998), Catalogo dei documenti sonori sulla musica somala, Centro Studi Somali — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/bitstream/2307/798/1/Catalogo%20dei%20documenti%20sonori%20sulla%20musica%20somala.pdf
Wikipedia, Somali literature

entries.definition: A short love lyric sung to a simple melody, created in 1943 according to Cabdullaahi Qarshe's own account (Giannattasio's catalogue; Goth) or 1943–1945 (Wikipedia), associated with Cabdi Deeqsi "Sinimo" (Giannattasio spells him Cabdi Shineemo) and his partner Khadiija Ciye Dharaar "Khadiija Balwo" in the Borama area, where the Borama Balwo Bands performed from 1944–46. The balwo brought secular love poetry to a mass public and was the seed of the heello and of modern Somali song.
entries.definitionSo: Gabay gaaban oo jacayl ah, laba ilaa afar tix, oo la heesaa; waxaa 1940-aadkii bilaabay Cabdi Deeqsi "Sinimo".
entries.etymology: The gloss "misfortune" is attested (Africa Diary 1964, via Wikipedia); the link to Arabic balwā is widely repeated but not found in a primary source here.
sources: Johnson, John William (1996), Heelloy: Modern Poetry and Songs of the Somali, Haan

Giannattasio, Francesco (1982–1998), Catalogo dei documenti sonori sulla musica somala, Centro Studi Somali — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/bitstream/2307/798/1/Catalogo%20dei%20documenti%20sonori%20sulla%20musica%20somala.pdf
Wikipedia, Balwo
Music in Africa, Somali music history (Goth) — https://www.musicinafrica.net/node/25169

entries.definition: A song: sung verse with a melody. In the classical division of Somali oral art, hees (light, sung, often danced verse) stands apart from maanso (weighty poetry recited rather than sung); modern hees since the heello has absorbed much of maanso's seriousness.
entries.definitionSo: Tix la heeso oo laxan leh; waxaa ka duwan maansada, oo ah gabay culus oo la tiriyo.
sources: Andrzejewski, B. W. & Lewis, I. M. (1964), Somali Poetry: An Introduction, Clarendon
Johnson, John William (1996), Heelloy

entries.definition: The weighty, authored poetry of the Somali tradition — gabay, geeraar, jiifto and related genres — composed by named poets and recited or chanted rather than sung and danced. The hees–maanso distinction is the classical dividing line of Somali oral literature.
entries.definitionSo: Gabayada culus ee abwaannada magacyada leh curiyaan oo la tiriyo; waxaa ka duwan heesta.
sources: Andrzejewski, B. W. & Lewis, I. M. (1964), Somali Poetry: An Introduction, Clarendon

entries.definition: The most prestigious classical Somali poetic genre: long alliterative lines in a fixed metre, chanted on a few pitches by the poet, used for politics, philosophy and dispute. Not sung as a song, but its metre and alliteration shaped how later sung forms were written.
entries.definitionSo: Gabayga waa tixda ugu sharafta badan maansada Soomaalida: tixo dhaadheer, miisaan go'an iyo higgaad.
sources: Andrzejewski, B. W. & Lewis, I. M. (1964), Somali Poetry: An Introduction, Clarendon
Banti, Giorgio & Giannattasio, Francesco (1996), Music and metre in Somali poetry, in Voice and Power (SOAS)

entries.definition: A classical genre of short lines, traditionally recited on horseback and linked to war and challenge; faster and more clipped than the gabay.
sources: Andrzejewski, B. W. & Lewis, I. M. (1964), Somali Poetry: An Introduction, Clarendon

entries.english: classical poem of short lines; a groove name in the studio
entries.definition: A classical Somali poetic genre of short lines, less formal than the gabay and often used for political and social argument in the twentieth century. The studio uses "jiifto" as the name of a light frame-drum groove preset.
sources: Andrzejewski, B. W. & Lewis, I. M. (1964), Somali Poetry: An Introduction, Clarendon

entries.english: women's poetry, song and dance genre
entries.definition: The principal genre of Somali women's verse: composed and performed by women, sung with clapping and drum and danced at weddings and celebrations; its texts range from praise and celebration to pointed social commentary.
entries.definitionSo: Gabayga haweenka Soomaaliyeed: waxaa la heesaa, la sacbiyaa, durbaan lagu garaacaa, oo arooska iyo xafladaha lagu ciyaaraa.
sources: Kapteijns, Lidwien with Maryan Omar Ali (1999), Women's Voices in a Man's World: Women and the Pastoral Tradition in Northern Somali Orature, c. 1899–1980, Heinemann
Andrzejewski, B. W. & Lewis, I. M. (1964), Somali Poetry

entries.english: western pastoral dance-song in a swinging rhythm
entries.definition: A dance-song of the camel-herding west (Somali Galbeed / Ogaden), performed with handclapping and foot-stamping, call-and-response verses and an off-beat accent; Xaange describes a dhaanto session in four phases and two-line verses interchangeable with the wiglo. Two origin accounts circulate: a Dervish-era revival (Johnson, via Wikipedia) and "first appeared in the 1930s, developed from hurbo" (Xaange). Revived as a popular stage and folk-dance form in the twentieth century and still widely performed.
entries.definitionSo: Ciyaar iyo hees reer-miyi ah oo galbeedka Soomaalida (Soomaali Galbeed) ka soo jeeda; sacab iyo cag-garaac, jawaab-celin, laxan dhaqaaqa.
entries.etymology: The link to the camel's gait is a widely repeated description, not a documented etymology.
sources: Xaange, Axmed Cartan (2014), Folk Songs from Somalia, Roma TrE-Press — https://romatrepress.uniroma3.it/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/folk-xapu.pdf

Giannattasio, Francesco (1982–1998), Catalogo dei documenti sonori sulla musica somala, Centro Studi Somali — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/bitstream/2307/798/1/Catalogo%20dei%20documenti%20sonori%20sulla%20musica%20somala.pdf
Wikipedia, Dhaanto
Dur-Dur Band, Bandcamp notes — https://dur-durbandint.bandcamp.com

entries.definition: Music and dance of spirit-possession ceremonies (the Horn-of-Africa zār complex), led by drums and repeated sung formulas that build toward trance. Regional forms carry their own names (for example mingis and boorane). A ritual repertoire, distinct from entertainment song.
entries.definitionSo: Muusig iyo ciyaar xafladaha saarka (ruuxaanta): durbaan iyo heeso soo noqnoqda oo gaarsiiya xaalad dareen-dhimis.
sources: Lewis, I. M. (1998), Saints and Somalis: Popular Islam in a Clan-based Society, Haan
Wikipedia, Zār

entries.definition: A dance-song performed across the central, eastern, northern and southern regions and towns (absent only in the west), also called sacab; the same technique as the dhaanto but a different rhythm pattern, traditionally staged when the rains come (Xaange). Giannattasio recorded it as a dance song (cayaar) of the Ceerigaabo region, Sanaag.
sources: Xaange, Axmed Cartan (2014), Folk Songs from Somalia, Roma TrE-Press — https://romatrepress.uniroma3.it/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/folk-xapu.pdf

Giannattasio, Francesco (1982–1998), Catalogo dei documenti sonori sulla musica somala, Centro Studi Somali — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/bitstream/2307/798/1/Catalogo%20dei%20documenti%20sonori%20sulla%20musica%20somala.pdf

entries.definition: Two documented senses: a dance song in the style of the Sanaag and Bari regions (Giannattasio recorded and transcribed "Tuma dheh, taa cusub dheh" from the Ceerigaabo area), and, in the south, a Banaadiri verse form used for bridges and verses (Hirsi 2023); Giannattasio adds that among the farmers a conch horn marks the passages of the shirib.
sources: Giannattasio, Francesco (1982–1998), Catalogo dei documenti sonori sulla musica somala, Centro Studi Somali — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/bitstream/2307/798/1/Catalogo%20dei%20documenti%20sonori%20sulla%20musica%20somala.pdf
Giannattasio, Francesco (1988), The study of Somali music: present state — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/handle/2307/984

Hirsi, Ibrahim (2023), Aweys Geedow Nuur "Diinle": Ciyow Biyaha Keen, a case study — https://wardheernews.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/Aweys-Geedow-Nuur-Diinles-Ciyow-Biyaha-Keen-A-Case-Study-By-Ibrahim-Hirsi.pdf
Giannattasio, Francesco (1987), Strumenti musicali — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/handle/2307/736

entries.definition: A northern Somali folk dance whose name means "big leap / big step", danced at most weddings and festive occasions and including a spinning move; one of the dances staged by diaspora troupes. Documented here only from journalism, not from the musicological sources.
sources: Twin Cities PBS (2018), Somali traditional dance 101 — https://www.tptoriginals.org/somali-traditional-dance-101/
Sahan Journal, Somali Museum dance troupe — https://sahanjournal.com/arts-culture/somali-museum-dance-troupe-minneapolis/

entries.definition: Dance, play or game; the general word for the group dances of the folk tradition (dhaanto, buraanbur, jaandheer and others), which are at once music, poetry and movement.
entries.definitionSo: Ciyaar: qoob-ka-ciyaar, ciyaar ama cayaar; erayga guud ee ciyaaraha dhaqanka.
sources: Zorc, R. David & Osman, Madina (1993), Somali–English Dictionary with English Index, Dunwoody

entries.definition: Songs sung to the rhythm of work — watering camels, pounding grain, weaving, herding — with simple repeating melodies and lines that set the pace of the task. A large and old part of the pastoral repertoire.
entries.definitionSo: Heeso la qaado marka hawl la qabanayo: geel-waraabin, hadhuudh-tun, reer-dhisid.
sources: Kapteijns, Lidwien (1999), Women's Voices in a Man's World, Heinemann
Andrzejewski, B. W. & Lewis, I. M. (1964), Somali Poetry

entries.definition: Songs for and by children: in Giannattasio's field classification hees carruureed covers lullabies (with the hoobeeya refrain) and children's songs; Galaal gives their line as eight syllables.
sources: Giannattasio, Francesco (1982–1998), Catalogo dei documenti sonori sulla musica somala, Centro Studi Somali — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/bitstream/2307/798/1/Catalogo%20dei%20documenti%20sonori%20sulla%20musica%20somala.pdf
Giannattasio, Francesco (1988), The study of Somali music: present state — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/handle/2307/984

entries.definition: A lullaby; also the soothing vocable ("hobeey, hobeeyo") that opens and fills the lullaby's lines. Mothers' lullabies are a recognised women's genre with their own tunes and imagery.
entries.definitionSo: Heesta hurdada ee carruurta lagu seexiyo; eraygan laftigiisa waa hadalka lagu hurdeysiiyo.
sources: Kapteijns, Lidwien (1999), Women's Voices in a Man's World, Heinemann

entries.definition: Patriotic and nationalist songs, a central strand of Somali music from the independence struggle of the 1950s onward; many of the best-known heello of Radio Hargeysa and Radio Muqdisho belong here.
entries.definitionSo: Heeso wadani ah oo ka hadlaya qaranka iyo xorriyadda; qayb muhiim ah oo heesaha 1950-aadkii.
sources: Johnson, John William (1996), Heelloy, Haan
Samatar, Said S. (1982), Oral Poetry and Somali Nationalism, Cambridge University Press

entries.definition: Religious poetry in praise of God, the Prophet and the saints, chanted in Arabic or Somali, often at Sufi gatherings; a devotional repertoire with its own melodic formulas, separate from secular song.
sources: Lewis, I. M. (1998), Saints and Somalis, Haan

entries.definition: The rhythmic communal chanting of God's names at Sufi gatherings, with swaying and sometimes frame drums; a devotional practice rather than entertainment music. Giannattasio's field spelling is digri: the intoned, rhythmically cadenced recitation of prayers of the Islamic orders (dariiqo), held to be "non-musical", so that verbs for singing such as qaadid and heesid are not used of its chants (qasiidooyin).
sources: Lewis, I. M. (1998), Saints and Somalis, Haan
Giannattasio, Francesco (1988), The study of Somali music: present state — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/handle/2307/984

Giannattasio, Francesco (1982–1998), Catalogo dei documenti sonori sulla musica somala, Centro Studi Somali — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/bitstream/2307/798/1/Catalogo%20dei%20documenti%20sonori%20sulla%20musica%20somala.pdf

entries.definition: A genre of religious and moral poetry in Somali, composed by sheikhs and learned men for teaching.
sources: Andrzejewski, B. W. & Lewis, I. M. (1964), Somali Poetry

entries.definition: The Somali stage play, which from the 1950s to the 1980s was the main vehicle for new songs: a spoken drama interleaved with heello written for it, performed by troupes such as Waaberi. Many classic qaraami songs were first heard in a riwaayad.
entries.definitionSo: Masraxiyadda Soomaalida oo hadal iyo heeso isugu jira; heeso badan oo caan ah ayaa riwaayado ka soo baxay.
sources: Johnson, John William (1996), Heelloy, Haan
Mumin, Hassan Sheikh (1974), Leopard Among the Women (Shabeelnaagood), trans. B. W. Andrzejewski, Oxford University Press

entries.definition: The oud: the short-necked lute that became the lead melodic instrument of Somali urban song. Giannattasio dates its introduction to 1948 and calls it the Yemeni lute (kaban; record keyword gambuus); Harvard's catalogue gives kaman/kaban; Goth credits one of the Borama Balwo Bands (before 1946) as the first to use an oud, and Cabdullaahi Qarshe with establishing it. Today's instrument is the fretless Arab oud. Qaraami is above all a kaban-and-voice music.
entries.definitionSo: Kaban: aalad xadhkaysan oo cuud ah, aan farac lahayn, oo laxanka heesaha qaraamiga hogaamin jirtay tan iyo 1940-aadkii.
entries.etymology: Not settled: the forms kaban/kamaan/kaman suggest a loan, but no fetched source gives the origin (the Arabic kamān "violin" proposal is unverified).
sources: Giannattasio, Francesco (1987), Strumenti musicali — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/handle/2307/736
Harvard Loeb Music Library blog, Somalia posts — https://archive.blogs.harvard.edu/loebmusic/tag/somalia/
Music in Africa, Somali music history (Goth) — https://www.musicinafrica.net/node/25169
Johnson, John William (1996), Heelloy, Haan

entries.definition: The traditional Somali bowl lyre: six strings over a bowl (xeero), tuned re4 re3 si3 la3 sol3 mi3 (Giannattasio 1987), played between the rivers and in the north (Berbera, Togdheer), and used to accompany the nuumbi ritual together with owlan drums; locally also called lumiya. The name is linked to the Semitic root knr; the Ethiopian krar is a cognate instrument, not a Somali spelling. The main indigenous string instrument before the kaban, now rare.
entries.definitionSo: Aalad xadhkaysan oo dhaqameed, lix xadhig iyo xeero, oo heesaha iyo nuumbiga lagu wehelin jiray ka hor kabanka.
sources: Giannattasio, Francesco (1987), Strumenti musicali — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/handle/2307/736

Giannattasio, Francesco (1982–1998), Catalogo dei documenti sonori sulla musica somala, Centro Studi Somali — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/bitstream/2307/798/1/Catalogo%20dei%20documenti%20sonori%20sulla%20musica%20somala.pdf
Giannattasio, Francesco (1988), The study of Somali music: present state — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/handle/2307/984

entries.definition: The drum: in Giannattasio's inventory durbaan (plural durbaanno) is the generic and the cylindrical-tubular drum, with named sub-types (yoome, jabbu or durbaan yar, nasar, masoonde, mokhoddon, tabuul, owlan, reeme); the frame drum or tambourine is the daf. Xaange notes that the women's haan dance is also called durbaan. The studio's durbaan voice plays three strokes: dum (low), tak (rim) and slap.
entries.definitionSo: Durbaan: aaladda garaacda ee ciyaaraha iyo heesaha u dhawaaqda; istuudiyadu waxay leedahay saddex dharbaaxo: dum, tak iyo dharbaaxo.
sources: Giannattasio, Francesco (1987), Strumenti musicali — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/handle/2307/736

Giannattasio, Francesco (1982–1998), Catalogo dei documenti sonori sulla musica somala, Centro Studi Somali — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/bitstream/2307/798/1/Catalogo%20dei%20documenti%20sonori%20sulla%20musica%20somala.pdf
Xaange, Axmed Cartan (2014), Folk Songs from Somalia, Roma TrE-Press — https://romatrepress.uniroma3.it/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/folk-xapu.pdf

entries.definition: Valve-shaped wooden clappers (garas, gulaan or deegaan wood), widespread throughout Somalia except some northern areas, struck as a louder substitute for handclapping (sacab) in dances such as xayaad; the metal clappers are called sharaq or biro (Giannattasio 1987).
sources: Giannattasio, Francesco (1987), Strumenti musicali — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/handle/2307/736

Giannattasio, Francesco (1982–1998), Catalogo dei documenti sonori sulla musica somala, Centro Studi Somali — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/bitstream/2307/798/1/Catalogo%20dei%20documenti%20sonori%20sulla%20musica%20somala.pdf

entries.definition: A horn or trumpet — traditionally a conch or animal horn blown for signalling and ceremony; in modern Somali also the word for brass instruments.
sources: Zorc, R. David & Osman, Madina (1993), Somali–English Dictionary

entries.definition: The guitar, electric and acoustic, a staple of the Radio Muqdisho and Waaberi band sound of the 1960s–1980s alongside the kaban.
sources: Ostinato Records (2017), Sweet As Broken Dates: Lost Somali Tapes from the Horn of Africa, liner notes

entries.definition: Piano and, by extension, the electric organs and synthesizer keyboards heard in Somali band recordings from the 1970s onward.
sources: Ostinato Records (2017), Sweet As Broken Dates, liner notes
Giannattasio, Francesco (1988), The study of Somali music: present state — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/handle/2307/984

entries.definition: The melody or tune of a song, as distinct from its words (erayo) and its poet; also used for the melodic setting a composer gives to a poem ("laxan u samee" — to set to a tune). In qaraami the laxan is typically pentatonic and sung in a free, ornamented line over the kaban.
entries.definitionSo: Laxan: luuqda ama heesta dhawaaqeed ee erayada lagu qaado; abwaanka iyo laxamiistaha waa kala duwan.
sources: Zorc, R. David & Osman, Madina (1993), Somali–English Dictionary
Johnson, John William (1996), Heelloy
entries.etymology: Spellings vary (laxan, lahan, laaxin); the Wikipedia articles on Somali, Somaliland and Djibouti music gloss the related agent noun inconsistently (lyricist / melody maker / songwriter). Zorc & Osman's dictionary still to be checked.

entries.english: vocal line, tune, manner of singing
entries.definition: The sung line or tune, with a stress on the voice's own shaping of it — a singer's luuq is their melodic manner. Often paired with laxan; also used for the chant tune of recited poetry.
entries.definitionSo: Luuq: codka iyo habka heesaa ugu qaado laxanka; waxaa kaloo loola jeedaa luuqda gabayga lagu tiriyo.
sources: Zorc, R. David & Osman, Madina (1993), Somali–English Dictionary

entries.definition: Voice, sound, vote; in music the singing voice and, in studio language, a vocal take (cod = the vocal track, as in the archive's session files). Cod wanaagsan — a fine voice.
entries.definitionSo: Cod: dhawaaqa qofka, codka heesaaga; istuudiyada waa duubista codka heesaaga.
sources: Zorc, R. David & Osman, Madina (1993), Somali–English Dictionary

entries.definition: The metre of a poem or song text: the fixed pattern of long and short vowels (moras) that each Somali genre follows. Scholars showed that these quantitative metres map onto musical rhythm when verse is sung or chanted.
entries.definitionSo: Miisaan: hannaanka shaqallada dhaadheer iyo gaagaaban ee tix walba oo nooc kasta oo maanso leeyahay.
sources: Banti, Giorgio & Giannattasio, Francesco (1996), Music and metre in Somali poetry, in R. J. Hayward & I. M. Lewis (eds.), Voice and Power, SOAS
Johnson, John William (1996), Heelloy

entries.definition: Alliteration: the rule that every line (or half-line) of a poem carries at least one word beginning with the poem's chosen sound. The defining ornament of Somali verse, kept in song lyrics as well. (Qaafiyad, from Arabic qāfiya, means rhyme, not alliteration; Samatar spells the term hikaad.)
entries.definitionSo: Higgaad: xaraf la doortay oo tix walba erey ku bilaabma ku jiro; qurxinta ugu weyn ee maansada iyo heesaha.
sources: Andrzejewski, B. W. & Lewis, I. M. (1964), Somali Poetry
Johnson, John William (1996), Heelloy
Wikipedia, Somali literature

entries.definition: The words of a song. In Somali practice the lyricist (abwaan) and the composer of the tune (laxamiiste) are usually credited separately, and the singer is a third name.
entries.definitionSo: Ereyada heesta; abwaanka qoray, laxamiistaha laxanka sameeyay iyo heesaaga qaaday waa saddex qof oo kala duwan.
sources: Zorc, R. David & Osman, Madina (1993), Somali–English Dictionary

entries.definition: To strike or beat; the drum beat itself. Garaaca durbaanka is drumming; by extension the rhythmic pulse a dance or song moves to.
entries.definitionSo: Garaac: wax garaacid; garaaca durbaanka waa dhawaaqa iyo xawaaraha ciyaarta lagu socdo.
sources: Zorc, R. David & Osman, Madina (1993), Somali–English Dictionary

entries.definition: Sound, and in musical talk a pitch or note; dhawaaqyada laxanka — the notes of a melody.
sources: Zorc, R. David & Osman, Madina (1993), Somali–English Dictionary

entries.definition: Music, as the general modern term (a loanword); traditional usage speaks instead of hees (song), ciyaar (dance) and the instruments.
sources: Zorc, R. David & Osman, Madina (1993), Somali–English Dictionary

entries.definition: Art, and specifically the Somali performing arts of song, music, dance and theatre as a public institution ("fanka Soomaaliyeed"). Its practitioners are fannaaniin.
sources: Zorc, R. David & Osman, Madina (1993), Somali–English Dictionary

entries.definition: An artist or performer — in practice a singer; fannaanad is the feminine form and fannaaniin the plural. The everyday word for a Somali musician.
entries.definitionSo: Fannaan: qof fanka ku shaqeeya, badanaa heesaa; fannaanad (dheddig), fannaaniin (wadar).
sources: Zorc, R. David & Osman, Madina (1993), Somali–English Dictionary

entries.definition: A singer (one who sings — heesaa from hees); heesaad for a woman singer.
sources: Zorc, R. David & Osman, Madina (1993), Somali–English Dictionary

entries.definition: A poet, and the usual credit for the author of a song's words; abwaan carries the prestige of the classical poet into modern song.
entries.definitionSo: Abwaan: gabyaa, qoraaga ereyada heesta.
sources: Zorc, R. David & Osman, Madina (1993), Somali–English Dictionary
Samatar, Said S. (1982), Oral Poetry and Somali Nationalism

entries.definition: Literally "one who creates": the creative artist in any of the verbal and musical arts — poet, composer, playwright, singer-songwriter. The broadest term for a maker of Somali art.
sources: Zorc, R. David & Osman, Madina (1993), Somali–English Dictionary

entries.definition: The composer who sets a poem to a tune (laxan); credited separately from the poet and the singer in Somali song. Spelled laxameyste and lahamiste in other sources, which disagree on the gloss (melody maker vs lyricist); kept as "composer" pending a dictionary check.
entries.definitionSo: Laxamiiste: qofka laxanka u sameeya ereyada abwaanka.
sources: Wikipedia, Music of Somaliland
Wikipedia, Music of Somalia
Zorc, R. David & Osman, Madina (1993), Somali–English Dictionary (to be checked)

entries.definition: An oud player (kaban + the agent suffix -le). The word was not found in the sources consulted for this glossary; Giannattasio's verbs for playing the kaban are tumid and garaacid.

entries.definition: The radio station of Hargeysa: a transmitter in 1941, "Radio Kudu" (Idaacadda Goodir) test broadcasts in 1942, the first live Somali broadcasts as "Hargeisa, Radio Somali" in 1945, and the name Radio Hargeisa from 1953 (Geeska; Wikipedia gives 1943). Its studios carried the balwo, the heello and the first qaraami stars to the Somali-speaking Horn; more than 10,000 cassettes and master tapes were hidden from destruction in 1988 and are among the most important documents of Somali music.
entries.definitionSo: Idaacadda Hargeysa, la aasaasay 1940-aadkii; waxay faafisay balwada, heellada iyo heesaha qaraamiga.

Most celebrated Somali singers of the 1960s–1980s were members, and its plays and songs reached the whole country.

entries.english: composer, oud pioneer (1924–1994 or 1997), "father of Somali music"
entries.definition: Composer, poet, singer and kaban player, born 1924 in Moshi (Tanganyika), died 1994 (Wikipedia) or 1997 (VIAF; Giannattasio gives "1924–1997?"), who set Somali verse to new melodies at Radio Hargeysa in the 1950s and is honoured as the father of modern Somali music; author of patriotic classics. Geeska (2025) names Beerdilaacshe, with Ciil and Laac, among the qaraam classics he originally composed; that is the only source found for the attribution, Jama Musse Jama's book description lists Beerdillaacshe without a composer, and no source consulted dates the melody.

entries.definition: Singer (born 1950) who rose in the Waaberi era, later recorded internationally (Real World Records, 1998), bringing Somali song to a world audience.

entries.definition: Answering: the leader–chorus alternation that structures dhaanto, buraanbur, work songs and fishing songs. The singer Xaaji Baalbaal named hurbo as the genre from which the "jiibdheer" dhaanto is said to derive, and he also sang a xurbo (literally "mixed"), placed between dhaanto and hirwo.

entries.definition: Arabic songs brought from Aden and played on phonographs by kabacad groups, with the music breaks filled by kasrad handclapping; Bashir Goth renders the name "the world is my poetry book". They dominated from 1939 to 1943, until the balwo was born, and in their final days Somali words replaced the Arabic while the music stayed the same.

entries.english: youth gathering where qaraami was sung
entries.definition: A popular gathering that drew large crowds of young people; leading qaraami poets were invited to perform at these and at weddings, despite the disapproval of elders and religious scholars (Wikipedia).

entries.definition: The Kabacad's name for composing in rotation: young poets seated in a circle improvised short verses in turn, one reciting a line and all chanting the final half-line (hooris) before the next went on. Wikipedia reports it as influenced by Quranic revision sessions.
sources: Wikipedia, Qaraami

entries.definition: The one-line format of the short verses improvised by qaraami poets in the subcis circle (Wikipedia).
sources: Wikipedia, Qaraami

entries.definition: Patriotic: Kapteijns describes waddani as "a whole sub-genre" of explicitly political modern song, the songs in which the discourse of soomaalinimo and Somali unity is most explicit.

entries.definition: Songs of praise for the leading women of early Islam, especially Faduumo (Fatima), which older women sing at a ceremony calling blessings on a woman about to give birth (Kapteijns 1999). entries.definition: The organ. It is Giannattasio's example of the two playing verbs: organka yeeri, "let the sound of the organ be heard", against heeskan organka ku tun, "play that song on the organ".
sources: Giannattasio, Francesco (1988), The study of Somali music: present state — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/handle/2307/984

entries.definition: To make an instrument "emit its own sound". As a verb for playing it is proper only to a few instruments, such as wind instruments, where manual action is involved only in the possible modulation (luuq) of the sound; Giannattasio finds that Somali classes instruments by this verb and tumid rather than by the four Western families.
sources: Giannattasio, Francesco (1988), The study of Somali music: present state — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/handle/2307/984
Giannattasio, Francesco (1987), Strumenti musicali — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/handle/2307/736

entries.definition: To beat or strike: the verb for playing strings (shareero, kaban), drums, mechanical aerophones such as the organ and accordion, handclaps, foot-stamping and clappers, as in heeskan organka ku tun, "play that song on the organ". Giannattasio adds that garaacid is sometimes used instead.
sources: Giannattasio, Francesco (1988), The study of Somali music: present state — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/handle/2307/984
Giannattasio, Francesco (1987), Strumenti musicali — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/handle/2307/736

entries.definition: More than "to sing", to perform a song, an already known piece. Giannattasio notes that it would be inappropriate to use it of the chants of the digri (qasiidooyin).
sources: Giannattasio, Francesco (1988), The study of Somali music: present state — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/handle/2307/984

entries.definition: One of the three performing practices into which Giannattasio divides Somali musical activity, with heesid and ciyaarid: composing and performing poetry.
sources: Giannattasio, Francesco (1988), The study of Somali music: present state — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/handle/2307/984

entries.definition: One of the three performing practices into which Giannattasio divides Somali musical activity, with gabyid and ciyaarid: singing songs. He also places the voice (cod) and the whistle (foori) of people and birds under this heading.
sources: Giannattasio, Francesco (1988), The study of Somali music: present state — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/handle/2307/984

entries.definition: One of the three performing practices into which Giannattasio divides Somali musical activity, with gabyid and heesid: playing and dancing, an action from which he finds the vocal and instrumental accompaniment of the dance difficult to separate.
sources: Giannattasio, Francesco (1988), The study of Somali music: present state — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/handle/2307/984

entries.definition: Multivocal singing. Giannattasio notes that jiib and jaan passed from nomadic practice into modern instrumental groups, where jiib names the melodic section and jaan the rhythmic one.
sources: Giannattasio, Francesco (1988), The study of Somali music: present state — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/handle/2307/984

entries.definition: The whistle, of people and birds alike, which Giannattasio places with the voice (cod) under singing (heesid) rather than among the instruments.
sources: Giannattasio, Francesco (1988), The study of Somali music: present state — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/handle/2307/984

entries.definition: Birds, whose song Giannattasio's figure of sound sources places with the voice and the whistle under singing (heesid). He notes the expression shimbirtu waa gabyaysaa, "the bird is singing".
sources: Giannattasio, Francesco (1988), The study of Somali music: present state — https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/handle/2307/984

entries.definition: Ululation; the catalogue glosses it as "trilli di glottide" (glottal trills) and records it with the buraanbur and in dances such as kabeebey.

entries.definition: A poet and lead singer: the catalogue glosses Axmedey Cabdi Gaashaan, who directed the National Theatre's folklore musicians, as "laashin (poeta, capo cantore)". Wikipedia, citing Luling, describes the Laashin of Afgooye composing and reciting at the same moment, with no prior preparation.

entries.definition: Quick, rhythmic handclapping that filled the music breaks when dunya diwani songs were performed (Bashir Goth).

entries.definition: A qaad-chewing session; Bashir Goth describes majlises at which men and women sat and sang dunya diwani songs together while girls danced the taxriig.

entries.definition: The intoxication of qaad; it occurs in the opening of the dheel recorded by Giannattasio, "Ama nala marqaan", glossed there as "or become drunk on qaad with us".

entries.definition: Somaliness. Kapteijns writes that the discourse of soomaalinimo and Somali unity informs both the love songs and the political songs of the modern hees, most explicitly the political ones.
